title: The environment and disease: association or causation?
headline: Nine viewpoints for judging whether an association in the data is likely to be causal -- still used today.
summary_short: Sir Austin Bradford Hill proposed a set of considerations -- such as strength, consistency, temporality and biological gradient -- for deciding when an observed association between an exposure and a disease is likely causal.
summary_detail:
Observational studies find associations far more often than they can prove causes. Hill's 1965 address set out viewpoints to weigh before inferring causation: the strength of the association, its consistency across studies and settings, its specificity, that the exposure comes before the disease (temporality), a biological gradient (more exposure, more effect), biological plausibility, coherence with other knowledge, supporting experimental evidence, and analogy with similar exposures.

Hill was explicit that these are viewpoints, not a checklist that yields a yes-or-no verdict; temporality is the one essential condition. Toxicologists and epidemiologists still use them in weight-of-evidence assessments.
key_findings: Association is not automatically causation
Strength, consistency, temporality and dose-gradient are central considerations
Considerations inform judgment; they are not a rigid checklist
limitations: A 1965 essay, so it predates modern methods such as omics and causal-inference modelling
No abstract is indexed on PubMed for this paper; this summary reflects its widely taught content
practical: When you hear 'linked to', ask which of these viewpoints the evidence actually meets
Look for a dose gradient and consistency across different kinds of studies

title: Why most published research findings are false
headline: A single 'significant' study is more likely to be wrong than right when studies are small, effects are small, and many relationships are tested.
summary_short: An influential essay argues that the chance a research claim is true depends on study power, bias, how many relationships were tested, and how many teams are chasing significance -- so one striking result deserves caution until replicated.
summary_detail:
The probability that a research claim is true depends on study power and bias, the number of other studies on the same question, and the ratio of true to no relationships among those probed in a field.

A finding is less likely to be true when studies are smaller, effect sizes are smaller, more relationships are tested with less pre-selection, designs and analyses are more flexible, there is greater financial or other interest, and more teams chase statistical significance. Simulations suggest that for most study designs and settings, a claim is more likely false than true, and that findings can often be accurate measures of prevailing bias.

The practical lesson for health headlines: weight replicated findings, large well-designed studies and consistent evidence across methods far above a single new result.
key_findings: Small studies, small effects and many tested relationships make false positives more likely
Flexible analyses and strong interests inflate apparent significance
Replication and convergence across methods matter more than any one result
limitations: A theoretical framework with simulations; real fields vary
Does not mean all research is wrong -- it explains when to be skeptical
practical: Ask whether a scary finding has been replicated and by whom
Prefer systematic reviews and consistent evidence over a single headline study

title: Particulate matter air pollution and cardiovascular disease: An update to the scientific statement from the American Heart Association
headline: Breathing fine particles for hours to weeks can trigger heart-related events; years of exposure add more.
summary_short: An American Heart Association expert panel concluded that fine particles (PM2.5) can trigger cardiovascular deaths and non-fatal events within hours to weeks, and that longer exposure carries even greater risk.
summary_detail:
The writing group reviewed the evidence since the AHA's 2004 statement and reached updated conclusions.

Exposure to PM2.5 over a few hours to weeks can trigger cardiovascular-related mortality and non-fatal events. Longer-term exposure (a few years) increases the risk of cardiovascular mortality to an even greater extent than short exposures, and reduces life expectancy in more polluted areas.

The statement also highlights clinical implications, which is why people with heart conditions are commonly advised to limit exposure on high-pollution days.
key_findings: Hours-to-weeks PM2.5 exposure can trigger cardiovascular events
Multi-year exposure raises cardiovascular mortality risk even more
Statement includes clinical implications for patients and clinicians
limitations: An expert consensus statement, not a single trial
Effects are larger for people who already have heart disease
practical: Indoor sources count: candles, incense and cooking smoke add particles too
If you have heart or lung disease, ask your clinician about high-pollution days

title: Sleep drives metabolite clearance from the adult brain
headline: In mice, sleep widened the space between brain cells by 60% and sped clearance of a waste protein.
summary_short: A Science study in live mice found the brain's interstitial space expands about 60% during sleep or anesthesia, boosting fluid flow and clearance of beta-amyloid -- a possible reason sleep is restorative.
summary_detail:
Using real-time tracer diffusion measurements and two-photon imaging in live mice, the team showed natural sleep or anesthesia was associated with a 60% increase in interstitial space and a striking increase in convective exchange between cerebrospinal and interstitial fluid.

This increased the rate of beta-amyloid clearance during sleep, suggesting the restorative function of sleep may be partly the enhanced removal of potentially neurotoxic waste products.

Important limit: this is a mouse study. It supports why sleep matters; it is not evidence that any product or routine 'detoxes' the human body.
key_findings: Interstitial space ~60% larger during sleep or anesthesia in mice
More convective fluid exchange and faster beta-amyloid clearance
Suggests a waste-clearance role for sleep
limitations: Mice, not humans
Does not show any 'detox' product or routine works
practical: Protect a consistent sleep window -- it is one of the best 'adding good' inputs
Log sleep in Daily to see how it lines up with your other numbers

title: Estimates and 25-year trends of the global burden of disease attributable to ambient air pollution: an analysis of data from the Global Burden of Diseases Study 2015
headline: Fine-particle air pollution ranked fifth among global mortality risk factors in 2015.
summary_short: Using satellite data, models and ground monitors, this analysis estimated that fine particles (PM2.5) caused about 4.2 million deaths in 2015 -- 7.6% of all deaths worldwide.
summary_detail:
The authors estimated population-weighted PM2.5 and ozone concentrations at about 11 km resolution by combining satellite estimates, chemical transport models and ground-level measurements.

Applying exposure-response functions for ischaemic heart disease, stroke, COPD, lung cancer and lower respiratory infections, they found ambient PM2.5 was the fifth-ranking mortality risk factor in 2015, responsible for 4.2 million deaths and 103.1 million disability-adjusted life-years.

The exposure-response curves are non-linear across the global range, which is why reductions matter at every level of exposure.
key_findings: PM2.5 caused an estimated 4.2 million deaths in 2015
Fifth-ranking global mortality risk factor
Modelled from satellites, chemical transport models and ground monitors
limitations: Modelled estimates with uncertainty (95% interval 3.7-4.8 million deaths)
Global averages -- your local air may be much cleaner or much worse
practical: Use a local air-quality reading to decide when to ventilate or go outside
A basic HEPA purifier is a reasonable step in high-PM areas

title: Environmental and heritable factors in the causation of cancer--analyses of cohorts of twins from Sweden, Denmark, and Finland.
headline: In 44,788 twin pairs, inherited genes explained only part of most common cancers -- the environment, in the broadest sense, did most of the work.
summary_short: Combining Swedish, Danish and Finnish twin registries, this study estimated how much of cancer at 11 sites came from heritable factors. Heritability was statistically significant for prostate (42%), colorectal (35%) and breast cancer (27%), and minor for most other types.
summary_detail:
Whether inherited genes drive ordinary (sporadic) cancer had been unclear. Twin studies help separate genes from environment: identical twins share all their genes and fraternal twins about half, while both usually grow up together. The authors combined 44,788 twin pairs from three Nordic registries, among whom 10,803 people developed at least one cancer, and modelled the relative importance of heritable and environmental factors at 11 cancer sites.

The twin of a person with cancer had higher odds of stomach, colorectal, lung, breast and prostate cancer. Statistically significant heritable effects were found for prostate (42%), colorectal (35%) and breast cancer (27%, with a wide interval of 4 to 41%). For most cancer types inherited genes made a minor contribution, and the authors concluded that the environment -- everything not inherited, including chance -- has the principal role in causing sporadic cancer.
key_findings: Heritable share: prostate 42%, colorectal 35%, breast 27% -- each with wide confidence intervals
For most cancer types, inherited genes made a minor contribution
Everything not inherited, including chance, had the principal role
limitations: 'Environment' here means everything not inherited, including chance; it does not say which exposures matter
Nordic populations of the 20th century; estimates may differ elsewhere
Estimates for individual cancer sites are imprecise
practical: Family history matters, but for most cancers it is not the main story
The exposome -- what you meet over a lifetime -- is where most of the room for change lies

title: Risks of Breast, Ovarian, and Contralateral Breast Cancer for BRCA1 and BRCA2 Mutation Carriers.
headline: Following nearly 10,000 women with harmful BRCA1 or BRCA2 variants, about 7 in 10 developed breast cancer by age 80.
summary_short: In a prospective cohort of 6,036 BRCA1 and 3,820 BRCA2 carriers, the cumulative chance of breast cancer by age 80 was 72% for BRCA1 and 69% for BRCA2, and of ovarian cancer 44% and 17%. Estimates rose with the number of affected relatives.
summary_detail:
Decisions for women with harmful BRCA1 or BRCA2 variants depend on reliable, prospective estimates. This study followed 9,856 carriers recruited in 1997-2011 through international cohorts, mostly in the UK, the Netherlands and France, for a median of five years.

The cumulative chance of breast cancer by age 80 was 72% for BRCA1 and 69% for BRCA2 carriers. Incidence rose quickly in early adulthood -- until ages 30 to 40 for BRCA1 and 40 to 50 for BRCA2 -- then stayed roughly constant. Ovarian cancer by 80 reached 44% (BRCA1) and 17% (BRCA2), and 20 years after a first breast cancer the chance of cancer in the other breast was 40% and 26%. Estimates were higher with more affected relatives and varied with where in the gene the variant sat.
key_findings: Breast cancer by age 80: about 72% (BRCA1) and 69% (BRCA2)
Ovarian cancer by age 80: about 44% (BRCA1) and 17% (BRCA2)
More affected relatives, and the variant's position in the gene, shifted the estimates
limitations: 94% of carriers were found through family clinics, which can over-represent families with many cancers
Median follow-up of five years; lifetime figures are projected from it
Applies to carriers of harmful variants -- about 1 in 300 to 500 women -- not the general population
practical: A strong family history is worth a conversation about genetic counseling
For carriers, screening and other options are planned with a specialist

title: Hormones and endocrine-disrupting chemicals: low-dose effects and nonmonotonic dose responses
headline: Some hormone-like chemicals can act at low doses in ways high-dose tests would not predict.
summary_short: The authors argue that for endocrine-disrupting chemicals, low-dose effects and non-monotonic dose-response curves are common -- challenging the simple rule that 'the dose makes the poison'.
summary_detail:
Low-dose effects were defined as those within the range of human exposures or below doses used in traditional toxicology studies. Non-monotonic curves are those where the slope changes sign within the tested dose range.

Using a weight-of-evidence approach on five examples and reviewing hundreds of cell, animal and epidemiology examples, the review concludes that non-monotonic responses and low-dose effects are remarkably common for natural hormones and endocrine disruptors, and discusses the mechanisms behind them.

The practical upshot is not alarm but humility: risk assessment based only on high-dose tests can miss real effects, especially in development.
key_findings: Low-dose and non-monotonic effects are common for hormones and EDCs
Mechanistic explanations exist (e.g., receptor and feedback dynamics)
Challenges a purely linear reading of dose-response
limitations: Regulatory interpretation of these findings is still debated
A review of the literature, not a new experiment
practical: Prefer reducing repeated, everyday exposures (food packaging, personal care) over one-off worry
Extra care around pregnancy and early childhood is well-founded

title: The Lancet Commission on pollution and health
headline: Pollution was linked to about 9 million premature deaths in 2015 -- roughly 1 in 6 worldwide.
summary_short: A major commission pulled together global evidence and concluded pollution -- above all air pollution -- is one of the largest preventable causes of disease and early death. The burden falls hardest in lower-income countries.
summary_detail:
The Commission reviewed the worldwide evidence on air, water, soil and chemical pollution and estimated its health toll.

It attributed about 9 million premature deaths in 2015 (16% of all deaths) to pollution, with air pollution the largest single contributor. Most of the burden falls on low- and middle-income countries, but every region is affected.

A central point for individuals: much of this burden is preventable through source control and clean-air measures, which is why local air quality, ventilation and filtration are worth attention.
key_findings: About 9 million premature deaths linked to pollution in 2015 (16% of all deaths)
Air pollution was the largest contributor
Burden is concentrated in lower-income countries but global
limitations: Population-level estimates -- not a prediction for any one person
A commission review synthesizes other studies rather than testing a hypothesis directly
practical: Check local air quality before outdoor exercise on hazy days
Ventilate and filter the rooms you spend the most time in

title: Adverse outcome pathways: a conceptual framework to support ecotoxicology research and risk assessment.
headline: The 'adverse outcome pathway' framework maps the whole chain from a chemical first touching a molecule in the body to a health effect showing up -- turning 'this changed a cell' into a structured, testable question instead of a scary-sounding fragment.
summary_short: This EPA-authored paper introduced the adverse outcome pathway (AOP): a structured chain of cause and effect running from a molecular initiating event (a chemical binding a specific receptor or protein), through a series of key events at the cell, tissue, and organ level, to an adverse outcome that actually matters for health. It's now a standard framework (adopted by the OECD) for organizing what a lab finding does and doesn't tell you.
summary_detail:
A common source of confusion in toxicology headlines is the gap between 'this chemical changed something in a cell' and 'this chemical harms health.' The adverse outcome pathway (AOP) framework, introduced in this paper, exists to make that gap explicit and testable rather than papered over.

An AOP lays out a documented chain: a molecular initiating event (e.g., a chemical binding to a specific hormone receptor) triggers a sequence of key events at increasing levels of biological organization -- cellular changes, then tissue-level effects, then organ-level effects -- culminating in an adverse outcome relevant to an individual or population (e.g., reduced fertility, a developmental effect). Each link in the chain can, in principle, be tested and either supported or weakened by evidence.

The practical value is that a lab finding like 'binds an estrogen receptor' or 'altered gene expression' can now be placed on a specific, named rung of a specific, named pathway, rather than treated as an isolated, alarming-sounding fact. If the downstream key events and the adverse outcome haven't been shown to follow, that's exactly what the AOP framework is built to make visible -- it doesn't let an early, molecular-level finding quietly stand in for a health outcome. The framework has since been adopted by the OECD as a formal way to organize toxicological knowledge and prioritize testing, especially for chemicals evaluated without animal studies.
key_findings: An adverse outcome pathway (AOP) links a molecular initiating event through intermediate 'key events' to a health-relevant adverse outcome, as a structured, testable chain
Each link in the chain can be independently supported or weakened by evidence, rather than the whole claim resting on one early-stage finding
The framework is now used by the OECD to organize toxicological knowledge and help prioritize which chemicals need further testing
limitations: A conceptual/methods framework, not a study with its own health-effect data -- its value is organizational, not a new finding about any specific chemical
Many AOPs are only partially documented; a molecular initiating event doesn't always have well-established downstream key events yet
practical: When a headline cites a lab finding ('binds a receptor', 'altered gene expression'), the AOP framework is the reason to ask what's actually been shown downstream, not just at that one early step
This is the same distinction the Engine Room's mechanism-vs-outcome framing draws on

title: EDC-2: The Endocrine Society's Second Scientific Statement on Endocrine-Disrupting Chemicals
headline: The Endocrine Society: exposures during development may lay the foundation for disease later in life.
summary_short: A professional society's consensus statement concluding that endocrine-disrupting chemicals are supported by strong mechanistic and animal evidence, consistent with human epidemiology -- especially for exposures during development.
summary_detail:
Five years after its first statement, the Society reviewed the topics where translational evidence is strongest, including obesity and diabetes and female and male reproduction.

It found a stronger understanding of how EDCs alter gene-environment interactions through physiological, cellular, molecular and epigenetic changes, with effects in exposed people and, in animals, their descendants. Causal links are supported by animal models and consistent with human correlational data.

The authors also flag caveats: differences in how animal experiments are run make broad conclusions difficult, and causality in humans must be inferred cautiously.
key_findings: Stronger mechanistic understanding since the 2009 statement
Developmental exposures may have lifelong effects
Animal evidence is consistent with human epidemiology
limitations: Causal inference in humans remains cautious, per the authors
Experimental designs vary across animal studies
practical: Simplify routines: fewer fragranced and plastic-contact products
Prioritize changes for pregnancy and young children

title: Complementing the genome with an "exposome": the outstanding challenge of environmental exposure measurement in molecular epidemiology
headline: The 'exposome' idea: measure the totality of a person's exposures, not just their genes.
summary_short: This editorial coined the term 'exposome' -- the totality of environmental exposures from conception onward -- and argued that measuring exposure is the outstanding challenge for understanding disease.
summary_detail:
Genome-wide studies were advancing quickly, but the author argued that our ability to measure environmental exposures -- including diet and lifestyle -- lagged behind.

The proposed remedy was to think in terms of an exposome: the totality of exposures across a life, complementing the genome, and to develop better tools to characterize it.

This is the conceptual root of the 'aggregate exposure' idea in this app: your picture is the running total across food, air, products and habits, not any single item.
key_findings: Introduced the term 'exposome'
Argues exposure measurement is the bottleneck
Frames exposure as a whole-life total
limitations: An editorial/concept paper, not a data study
practical: Think in running totals: small repeated exposures add up
Every log you add improves your own exposure picture

title: Per- and Polyfluoroalkyl Substance Toxicity and Human Health Review: Current State of Knowledge and Strategies for Informing Future Research
headline: PFAS are linked to immune, thyroid, liver, lipid and other effects -- but most of the family is barely studied.
summary_short: This review found associations between specific PFAS and effects on immune and thyroid function, liver disease, lipid and insulin regulation, kidney disease, reproduction and cancer. Toxicity data exist for only a handful of the hundreds of PFAS in use.
summary_detail:
Most toxicity data cover a few 'legacy' compounds such as PFOA and PFOS. For these, epidemiology has found associations with altered immune and thyroid function, liver disease, lipid and insulin dysregulation, kidney disease, adverse reproductive and developmental outcomes, and cancer, and many effects agree with animal data.

The authors stress that PFAS differ greatly in how they move through and leave the body (toxicokinetics), including by sex, species and life stage, and that hundreds of other PFAS lack toxicity data. They propose newer approaches -- read-across, molecular dynamics, protein modelling -- and suggest an appropriate degree of precaution.
key_findings: Associations with immune, thyroid, liver, lipid, kidney, reproductive outcomes and cancer for some PFAS
Data are concentrated on a few legacy compounds
Toxicokinetics differ widely between PFAS and between people
limitations: Many findings are associations, not proof of causation in people
Data gaps for most PFAS in commerce
practical: Where easy, choose alternatives to stain-resistant and grease-proof coatings
Check your water utility's report for PFAS testing results

title: Low-level environmental lead exposure and children's intellectual function: an international pooled analysis
headline: In 1,333 children, higher blood lead meant lower IQ -- and the steepest drop was at the lowest levels.
summary_short: Pooling seven long-running cohorts, researchers found IQ fell as blood lead rose, even below 10 micrograms/dL, with a larger drop per unit of lead at the lowest exposures.
summary_detail:
The analysis combined data from 1,333 children in seven international population-based cohorts followed from infancy to age 5-10. After adjustment, blood lead was inversely related to full-scale IQ.

Increasing blood lead from 2.4 to 30 micrograms/dL was associated with a 6.9-point IQ decrement. The decrement was steeper at low levels: 3.9 points from 2.4 to 10, 1.9 from 10 to 20, and 1.1 from 20 to 30 micrograms/dL.

Children whose maximum blood lead stayed below 7.5 micrograms/dL still showed a lead-associated deficit.
key_findings: 6.9 IQ-point decrement across 2.4 to 30 micrograms/dL
Steeper per-unit effect at lower blood lead
Deficit seen even when blood lead stayed below 7.5 micrograms/dL
limitations: Observational; residual confounding is possible
Group-level effect sizes, not individual prediction
practical: Ask your utility about lead service lines and test water in older homes
Wet-clean dust and keep shoes at the door in homes built before 1978

title: Cancer etiology. Variation in cancer risk among tissues can be explained by the number of stem cell divisions.
headline: Across tissue types, lifetime cancer rates tracked the number of stem-cell divisions -- a reminder that chance copying errors play a real part.
summary_short: Comparing many tissue types, lifetime cancer risk correlated strongly (0.81) with the total number of divisions of the stem cells that maintain each tissue. The authors estimated that only about a third of the variation between tissues is attributable to environment or inheritance.
summary_detail:
Some tissues give rise to cancer millions of times more often than others. Tomasetti and Vogelstein compared lifetime cancer risk across many tissue types with the total number of divisions made by the normal stem cells that renew each tissue, and found a strong correlation (0.81). They concluded that only about a third of the variation in cancer risk among tissues is attributable to environmental factors or inherited predispositions, with the majority reflecting random mutations as DNA is copied in normal stem cells.

The paper was widely misread as saying that most cancer cases are 'bad luck'. It addresses differences between tissues, not the share of cases that prevention could reach -- a different question, answered by estimates such as the American Cancer Society's. Both can be true: chance plays a real part in every tissue, and exposures still shift the odds.
key_findings: Lifetime cancer risk across tissues correlated 0.81 with total stem-cell divisions
About a third of the variation between tissues was attributed to environment or inheritance
Random DNA-copying errors help explain why some tissues develop cancer far more often
limitations: About differences between tissues, not the preventable share of cancer cases
Stem-cell numbers for some tissues were uncertain estimates
Its interpretation was widely debated after publication
practical: A cancer can arise without anyone having done anything to cause it
Prevention still matters: exposures shift the odds on top of chance

title: Acetaminophen-induced acute liver failure: results of a United States multicenter, prospective study.
headline: Acetaminophen is the single leading cause of acute liver failure in the US -- median overdose was 24 g, about 48 extra-strength tablets, and 38% of unintentional cases involved taking two or more acetaminophen products at once without realizing it.
summary_short: A 6-year prospective study across 22 US transplant centers found acetaminophen overdose caused 42% of all acute liver failure cases -- more than any other cause. Nearly half were unintentional, often from combining a plain acetaminophen product with a second medicine (like a cold remedy or a narcotic combination pill) that also contained it, without the person realizing the dose was stacking.
summary_detail:
Researchers tracked 662 consecutive acute liver failure patients at 22 US tertiary care centers over six years. Acetaminophen was responsible for 275 cases (42%) -- more than any other single cause, and the share was rising over the study period (28% of ALF cases in 1998 to 51% by 2003).

The median dose ingested was 24 g, equivalent to about 48 extra-strength (500 mg) tablets -- far above the FDA's current maximum recommended adult dose of 3-4 g per day. Just under half (48%) of cases were unintentional overdoses, not suicide attempts. Within that unintentional group, 38% had taken two or more acetaminophen-containing products at the same time, and 63% were also using a narcotic-combination pain reliever -- many of which contain acetaminophen as a second ingredient a person might not think to count. 81% reported taking it for an ongoing pain condition, not a one-time slip.

Acetaminophen hepatotoxicity is a clean, well-characterized example of dose-dependent injury: below the recommended dose it's one of the most-used, best-tolerated over-the-counter medicines in the world; well above it, it's the leading cause of a life-threatening condition. The authors' practical recommendation was straightforward: better labeling and patient/pharmacist education to reduce simultaneous multi-product use.
key_findings: Acetaminophen caused 42% of acute liver failure cases across 22 US centers over 6 years -- more than any other identified cause
Median overdose was 24 g (about 48 extra-strength tablets), well above the ~3-4 g/day recommended maximum
38% of unintentional overdoses involved combining two or more acetaminophen-containing products at once
limitations: Tertiary-center liver failure patients are the most severe end of the spectrum -- most acetaminophen use never approaches this
A US study from the mid-1990s-2000s; labeling and combination-product warnings have changed somewhat since
practical: Check whether a second medicine (cold/flu remedy, prescription pain reliever) also lists acetaminophen before adding a plain acetaminophen product on top
The FDA's current adult maximum is 3,000-4,000 mg/day across ALL sources combined, not per product

title: Ultra-Processed Diets Cause Excess Calorie Intake and Weight Gain: An Inpatient Randomized Controlled Trial of Ad Libitum Food Intake
headline: Twenty adults ate about 500 kcal/day more on an ultra-processed diet than on an unprocessed one -- with matched menus.
summary_short: In a two-week-each crossover trial at the NIH Clinical Center, people given ultra-processed meals ate about 508 more kcal/day and gained weight; on the unprocessed diet they lost weight.
summary_detail:
Twenty weight-stable adults lived in the NIH Clinical Center and were randomized to ultra-processed or unprocessed diets for two weeks, then switched. Meals were designed to match for presented calories, energy density, macronutrients, sugar, sodium and fiber, and people could eat as much or little as they wanted.

Energy intake was 508 kcal/day higher on the ultra-processed diet, with more carbohydrate and fat but not protein. Participants gained 0.9 kg on the ultra-processed diet and lost 0.9 kg on the unprocessed one.

The authors conclude that limiting ultra-processed foods may help prevent and treat obesity.
key_findings: +508 kcal/day on the ultra-processed diet (p=0.0001)
+0.9 kg vs -0.9 kg over two weeks
Weight change tracked energy intake (r=0.8)
limitations: Only 20 people and 4 weeks in a controlled setting
Shows effect on eating, not on additive toxicity
practical: Swapping a few packaged items for whole foods is a realistic first step
Try the cereal-aisle swap from your starter quests

title: Bisphenol S and F: A Systematic Review and Comparison of the Hormonal Activity of Bisphenol A Substitutes.
headline: Bisphenol S and F -- the most common 'BPA-free' replacements -- turned out to be about as hormonally active as BPA itself across 32 pooled studies.
summary_short: A systematic review pooling 25 in vitro and 7 in vivo studies compared the hormonal activity of bisphenol S (BPS) and bisphenol F (BPF) -- two chemicals widely substituted for BPA in 'BPA-free' products -- directly against BPA. Their estrogenic, antiestrogenic, androgenic, and antiandrogenic potency landed in the same order of magnitude as BPA, not meaningfully lower.
summary_detail:
As BPA drew regulatory and consumer scrutiny, many manufacturers reformulated products to remove it, often labeling the result 'BPA-free.' The most common replacements -- bisphenol S (BPS) and bisphenol F (BPF) -- are themselves bisphenols, sharing BPA's core two-ring structure with a different bridging group between them.

The authors systematically reviewed the available literature (32 studies total: 25 in vitro, 7 in vivo) comparing BPS and BPF's hormonal activity to BPA's. Both showed potency 'in the same order of magnitude and of similar action as BPA' across estrogenic, antiestrogenic, androgenic, and antiandrogenic pathways. BPS specifically showed potency similar to estradiol itself in some membrane-mediated signaling pathways relevant to cell proliferation and differentiation. In vivo, both substitutes altered organ weights and reproductive endpoints in ways comparable to BPA exposure.

The authors' conclusion is direct: based on the literature to date, BPS and BPF are about as hormonally active as BPA and have endocrine-disrupting effects of their own. This is the foundational paper behind what toxicologists now call 'regrettable substitution' -- swapping a scrutinized chemical for a close structural relative that hasn't drawn the same attention yet, without necessarily changing the underlying biological activity.
key_findings: BPS and BPF potency landed in the same order of magnitude as BPA across estrogenic, antiestrogenic, androgenic, and antiandrogenic activity
BPS showed estradiol-like potency in some membrane-mediated signaling pathways
In vivo studies found altered organ weights and reproductive endpoints comparable to BPA
limitations: Most of the underlying evidence (25 of 32 studies) is in vitro, not human data
A synthesis of existing studies, not a new human exposure study -- inherits whatever gaps the underlying literature has
practical: A 'BPA-free' label describes what's absent, not what replaced it -- worth checking whether the replacement is itself a bisphenol
The same heat/reheating-avoidance habits that reduce BPA exposure apply to its bisphenol relatives too

title: The benefits and harms of breast cancer screening: an independent review.
first_author: Independent UK Panel on Breast Cancer Screening
study_type: Independent review with meta-analysis of randomised trials
headline: For every 10,000 women invited to screening from age 50 for 20 years: about 43 breast cancer deaths prevented, and about 129 cancers overdiagnosed.
summary_short: An independent panel reviewing 11 randomised trials estimated a 20% relative reduction in breast cancer mortality for women invited to screening, and roughly one death prevented for about every three cancers overdiagnosed -- cancers that would never otherwise have come to light.
summary_detail:
Whether breast screening does more good than harm had been debated for years. An independent panel, focused on the UK programme (women aged 50 to 70 invited every three years), reviewed published studies and expert evidence. In a meta-analysis of 11 randomised trials, women invited to screening had a relative risk of breast cancer death of 0.80 compared with controls -- a 20% relative reduction, which the panel judged still reasonable despite the trials' age.

Overdiagnosis -- cancers found at screening that would not have become clinically apparent in a woman's lifetime -- was best estimated from three trials, at about 11% of cancers diagnosed in invited women over the long term. Applied to the UK, for every 10,000 women invited from age 50 for 20 years, about 43 breast cancer deaths would be prevented and 129 cancers overdiagnosed. The panel stressed the uncertainty and called for clear, objective information so women can make informed decisions.
key_findings: Invitation to screening: 20% relative reduction in breast cancer mortality (relative risk 0.80)
Per 10,000 women invited from 50 for 20 years: about 43 deaths prevented and 129 cancers overdiagnosed
Roughly one death prevented for every three overdiagnosed cancers
limitations: The trials were done decades ago; screening and treatment have changed
Estimates of overdiagnosis vary widely by method
UK programme details (ages 50 to 70, every three years) differ from US recommendations
practical: Screening decisions deserve both numbers, out of the same number of people
Ask what is known about benefit and overdiagnosis at your age

title: HPV Vaccination and the Risk of Invasive Cervical Cancer.
headline: Among 1.7 million Swedish girls and women, HPV vaccination before age 17 was linked to about 88% fewer cervical cancers.
summary_short: Following 1,672,983 girls and women aged 10 to 30 in Swedish registers (2006-2017), cervical cancer occurred in 47 per 100,000 vaccinated and 94 per 100,000 unvaccinated. After full adjustment the incidence rate ratio was 0.12 for vaccination before 17 and 0.47 for vaccination at 17 to 30.
summary_detail:
Trials had shown that the quadrivalent HPV vaccine prevents high-grade cervical lesions, but direct evidence on invasive cancer was lacking. Using nationwide demographic and health registers, this study followed 1,672,983 Swedish girls and women aged 10 to 30 from 2006 through 2017, up to their 31st birthday.

Cervical cancer was diagnosed in 19 vaccinated and 538 unvaccinated women -- a cumulative incidence of 47 versus 94 per 100,000. Adjusted for age, calendar year, county and parental characteristics, the incidence rate ratio was 0.37 overall, 0.12 for girls vaccinated before 17 and 0.47 for women vaccinated at 17 to 30. Infections are among the cancer causes prevention can reach most directly, and the earliest vaccination showed the largest difference.
key_findings: Cumulative cervical cancer incidence: 47 vs 94 per 100,000 (vaccinated vs not)
Fully adjusted rate ratio 0.12 when vaccinated before age 17
Rate ratio 0.47 when vaccinated at 17 to 30
limitations: Observational: vaccinated and unvaccinated women may differ in ways registers cannot capture
Follow-up only to age 31, when cervical cancer is still uncommon
Quadrivalent vaccine in Sweden; other vaccines and settings may differ
practical: HPV vaccination is one of the most direct cancer-prevention steps available
Vaccination before exposure to the virus showed the largest difference

title: Association of Leisure-Time Physical Activity With Risk of 26 Types of Cancer in 1.44 Million Adults.
headline: Across 1.44 million adults, more leisure-time activity was linked to lower rates of 13 cancers, breast cancer included.
summary_short: Pooling 12 US and European cohorts with 186,932 cancers, high versus low leisure-time physical activity was associated with lower risk of 13 cancer types, including breast (HR 0.90), colon (0.84) and endometrial (0.79), mostly regardless of body size or smoking.
summary_detail:
Physical activity was known to lower heart disease and overall mortality; its relation to specific cancers was less clear. This analysis pooled 12 prospective cohorts from the US and Europe -- 1.44 million adults with a median age of 59 -- and compared people at the 90th and 10th percentiles of moderate-to-vigorous leisure-time activity.

Higher activity was associated with lower risk of 13 of 26 cancers, from esophageal adenocarcinoma (hazard ratio 0.58) and liver (0.73) to colon (0.84) and breast (0.90). Adjusting for body mass index weakened some associations, but 10 of 13 remained, and results were similar for normal-weight and overweight people. Activity was associated with higher risk of malignant melanoma (1.27) and, slightly, prostate cancer (1.05).
key_findings: High vs low activity: lower risk of 13 cancers, including breast (HR 0.90) and colon (0.84)
10 of 13 associations held after adjusting for body mass index
Higher risk of melanoma (1.27) and, slightly, prostate cancer (1.05)
limitations: Self-reported activity, measured once at baseline
Observational: more active people may differ in other ways
Compares the 90th with the 10th percentile, a wide contrast
practical: Activity is a lever that shows up across many cancers, breast included
Associations held at any body size, so activity counts whether or not weight changes

title: Breast cancer and breastfeeding: collaborative reanalysis of individual data from 47 epidemiological studies in 30 countries, including 50302 women with breast cancer and 96973 women without the disease.
first_author: Collaborative Group on Hormonal Factors in Breast Cancer
headline: Each 12 months of breastfeeding was linked to about 4% lower relative risk of breast cancer, on top of about 7% for each birth.
summary_short: Pooling individual data from 47 studies in 30 countries, including 50,302 women with breast cancer, the relative risk of breast cancer fell 4.3% for every 12 months of breastfeeding, in addition to 7.0% for each birth, with similar effects across countries and personal characteristics.
summary_detail:
Childbearing was known to lower breast cancer risk, but the separate contribution of breastfeeding was unclear. The Collaborative Group gathered and reanalysed individual data from 47 studies in 30 countries -- 50,302 women with invasive breast cancer and 96,973 without.

Women with breast cancer had fewer births on average (2.2 vs 2.6), were less likely to have breastfed (71% vs 79% of mothers) and breastfed for less time in total (9.8 vs 15.6 months). Relative risk fell 4.3% for every 12 months of breastfeeding, in addition to 7.0% for each birth, with similar estimates by age, menopausal status, ethnic origin and country. The authors estimated that fewer births and shorter breastfeeding explain much of the higher breast cancer incidence in high-income countries.
key_findings: 4.3% lower relative risk per 12 months of breastfeeding
7.0% lower relative risk per birth, independently
Effects were similar across countries and personal characteristics
limitations: Breastfeeding history was mostly reported years later
Observational: breastfeeding can reflect other differences between women
Population estimates; they say nothing about why any one woman's cancer occurred
practical: Support for breastfeeding -- at work and at home -- is a population-level prevention lever
It is one factor among many; not breastfeeding is never a reason for blame

title: Radon in homes and risk of lung cancer: collaborative analysis of individual data from 13 European case-control studies
headline: Lung-cancer risk rose about 8% per 100 Bq/m3 of home radon -- with no safe threshold found.
summary_short: Pooling 13 European studies (7,148 cases, 14,208 controls), researchers found lung cancer risk increased in a straight line with measured home radon, and the effect was clearest for smokers.
summary_detail:
Relative risk rose 8.4% per 100 Bq/m3 of measured radon (16% after correcting for measurement uncertainty). The dose-response looked linear with no threshold and remained significant even among people whose homes measured under 200 Bq/m3.

By age 75, absolute lung-cancer risk at 0, 100 and 400 Bq/m3 was estimated at about 0.4%, 0.5% and 0.7% for lifelong non-smokers, and roughly 25 times higher (10%, 12%, 16%) for cigarette smokers. Radon was estimated to cause about 2% of cancer deaths in Europe.
key_findings: +8.4% lung-cancer risk per 100 Bq/m3 (16% corrected)
Linear dose-response with no threshold seen
Absolute risk far higher for smokers
limitations: Case-control design relies on recalled home history
European homes; local radon varies widely
practical: A home radon test kit is inexpensive and is your boss quest
If a test is high, a mitigation contractor can lower it

title: Familial breast cancer: collaborative reanalysis of individual data from 52 epidemiological studies including 58,209 women with breast cancer and 101,986 women without the disease.
first_author: Collaborative Group on Hormonal Factors in Breast Cancer
headline: Eight in nine women who develop breast cancer have no affected mother, sister or daughter -- and most women with an affected relative never develop it.
summary_short: In pooled data on 58,209 women with breast cancer, one, two or three affected first-degree relatives raised breast cancer risk 1.8, 2.9 and 3.9 times. Estimated cumulative incidence to age 80 was about 7.8%, 13.3% and 21.1% with zero, one and two affected relatives.
summary_detail:
Family history is a familiar factor in breast cancer, but no single study had been large enough to describe it reliably over a woman's life. The Collaborative Group reanalysed individual data from 52 studies: 58,209 women with breast cancer and 101,986 without.

About 12.9% of women with breast cancer, and 7.3% of controls, had at least one affected mother, sister or daughter. Compared with no affected relative, risk ratios were 1.80 for one, 2.93 for two and 3.90 for three or more, and were highest at young ages. In absolute terms for high-income countries, the estimated cumulative incidence to age 80 was 7.8%, 13.3% and 21.1% for zero, one and two affected relatives. In the authors' summary, eight out of nine women who develop breast cancer have no affected first-degree relative, and most women who have one will never develop the disease.
key_findings: Risk ratios 1.80, 2.93 and 3.90 for one, two and three or more affected relatives
Cumulative incidence to 80: 7.8% (none), 13.3% (one), 21.1% (two)
Eight in nine women who develop breast cancer have no affected first-degree relative
limitations: Family history was self-reported
Absolute figures are for high-income countries around 2000
Does not separate inherited variants such as BRCA1/2 from shared family environment
practical: Know your family's history -- it is where a risk assessment starts
Screening by age matters because most cases occur without a family history

title: Microplastics and Nanoplastics in Atheromas and Cardiovascular Events
headline: Plastic particles found in artery plaque were associated with more heart attacks, strokes and deaths over about 34 months.
summary_short: In 257 patients followed after carotid surgery, those whose plaque contained micro- or nanoplastics had a higher rate of heart attack, stroke or death. It shows association, not proof that plastics caused the events.
summary_detail:
Researchers analyzed carotid plaque removed from 304 patients (257 completed follow-up of about 33.7 months) using pyrolysis-gas chromatography-mass spectrometry and electron microscopy. Polyethylene was found in 58.4% of patients and polyvinyl chloride in 12.1%.

Patients with plastics detected had a higher risk of the composite outcome of heart attack, stroke or death (hazard ratio 4.53; 95% CI 2.00-10.27).

Because it is observational, the study cannot show that plastics caused the events -- people with plastics in plaque may differ in other ways.
key_findings: Polyethylene in 58.4% of plaques; PVC in 12.1%
Hazard ratio 4.53 for heart attack, stroke or death
Jagged-edged particles seen among plaque macrophages
limitations: Observational -- association, not causation
Patients already had carotid disease; results may not generalize
practical: Reduce the biggest everyday contact routes first: heating food in plastic, single-use bottles
Treat this as a reason to learn, not to worry

title: American Cancer Society nutrition and physical activity guideline for cancer survivors.
headline: The American Cancer Society's guideline for survivors centres on body weight, physical activity, diet and alcohol, alongside treatment.
summary_short: Written for survivors, their families and clinicians, this guideline gives cancer-specific recommendations on body weight, physical activity, diet and alcohol intake, drawn from systematic reviews, pooled cohorts and large trials published since 2012.
summary_detail:
With a five-year relative survival rate of 68% across all cancers and more than 16.9 million survivors in the United States, the American Cancer Society set out evidence-based recommendations for life after a diagnosis. The evidence -- systematic reviews, meta-analyses, pooled analyses of cohort studies and large randomised trials published since 2012 -- suggests that diet, physical activity and body weight may affect recurrence and survival, though much of it is observational.

Beyond the recommendations themselves, the guideline covers nutrition and activity during treatment, long-term side effects, other health conditions, patient-reported outcomes and health disparities, with attention to what makes the advice possible to follow, and to care coordination and counseling after diagnosis.
key_findings: Recommendations cover body weight, physical activity, diet and alcohol for survivors
Evidence suggests these may affect recurrence and survival; much of it is observational
Attention to side effects, other conditions and access, not only to targets
limitations: Much of the evidence for individual recommendations is observational
Population guidance; individual plans belong with the care team
The strength of evidence varies by cancer type
practical: Bring questions about activity, diet and alcohol to the care team
Practical support -- a walking partner, shared meals -- can make the advice easier to follow

title: Alcohol, tobacco and breast cancer--collaborative reanalysis of individual data from 53 epidemiological studies, including 58,515 women with breast cancer and 95,067 women without the disease.
headline: Each daily drink was linked to about 7% higher relative risk of breast cancer -- and once alcohol was accounted for, smoking showed no independent link.
summary_short: Pooling 53 studies with 58,515 women with breast cancer, relative risk rose 7.1% for each additional 10 g of alcohol a day, roughly one drink. Among women who did not drink, smoking was not associated with breast cancer. About 4% of breast cancers in high-income countries were estimated to be attributable to alcohol.
summary_detail:
Alcohol and tobacco use go together, and earlier studies had not always separated them. This collaborative reanalysis pooled individual data covering more than 80% of the relevant worldwide evidence: 58,515 women with invasive breast cancer and 95,067 controls from 53 studies.

Compared with no alcohol, relative risk was 1.32 at 35 to 44 g a day and 1.46 at 45 g or more, rising 7.1% for every additional 10 g a day -- about one drink -- equally in smokers and non-smokers. Among the 22,255 cases and 40,832 controls who drank no alcohol, smoking was not associated with breast cancer (relative risk 1.03 for ever-smokers). If causal, alcohol would account for about 4% of breast cancers in high-income countries and very few where women drank little.
key_findings: +7.1% relative risk per additional 10 g of alcohol a day (about one drink)
Relative risk 1.46 at 45 g a day or more, compared with none
Smoking had little or no independent effect on breast cancer once alcohol was accounted for
limitations: Drinking was self-reported, mostly in case-control studies
Relative figures; the absolute change depends on a woman's baseline
Alcohol's other effects -- on the liver, other cancers and the heart -- were outside this analysis
practical: Drinking less lowers alcohol's contribution at every level
Smoking still matters for many other cancers and for anyone breathing the smoke

title: The exposome and health: Where chemistry meets biology.
headline: Mapping the exposome on the scale of the human genome: why researchers argue it is now possible, and needed.
summary_short: This review argues that research and regulation fail to address the chemical complexity of daily life, and that high-resolution mass spectrometry and network science now allow first steps toward a systematic, agnostic assessment of the exposome.
summary_detail:
Chemicals are usually studied one at a time, while people meet synthetic chemicals, dietary constituents, psychosocial stressors and physical factors together. The exposome concept tries to capture that whole range, along with the body's biological responses to it.

The authors describe the technologies that make a systematic approach plausible -- high-resolution mass spectrometry that detects many chemicals in a single sample, and network science that relates exposures to biology -- and argue that, given the increasingly recognised dominant role of non-genetic factors in disease, an effort to characterise the exposome at a scale comparable to that of the human genome is warranted.
key_findings: Research and regulation still mostly address chemicals one at a time
High-resolution mass spectrometry and network science enable first steps toward measuring the exposome
Calls for an exposome effort on the scale of the human genome
limitations: A perspective review rather than new data
Measuring a lifetime of changing exposures remains far harder than reading a genome
The approach is still largely at the research stage
practical: Treat claims to 'measure everything you're exposed to' with care
Studying many exposures together is where this science is heading

title: Helping Doctors and Patients Make Sense of Health Statistics
headline: A '25% reduction' in risk can mean one fewer person in 1,000 -- and many doctors, journalists and patients misread it.
summary_short: This review shows that statistical illiteracy is common among patients, journalists and physicians, and that how numbers are framed -- relative instead of absolute -- can make benefits look big and harms look small.
summary_detail:
The authors argue that many people, including professionals, do not understand what health statistics mean. One example from the paper: a statement that mammography screening reduces the risk of dying from breast cancer by 25% actually means 1 fewer woman out of 1,000 dies of the disease. Another: higher survival rates with cancer screening do not by themselves imply longer life.

They provide evidence that statistical illiteracy is common to patients, journalists and physicians; that it is created by non-transparent framing of information (sometimes unintentional, sometimes deliberate); and that it can have serious consequences for health.

The remedy is not more fear or more reassurance but transparent numbers: absolute risks, natural frequencies ('X out of 1,000 people'), and clear reference groups. That is the habit this app's risk tools are built to practice.
key_findings: Relative-risk framing can hide how small an absolute change is
Statistical illiteracy is common among patients, journalists and physicians
Transparent formats (absolute numbers, 'out of 1,000') help everyone
limitations: A review of the literature, not a new experiment
Its screening examples illustrate framing; they are not advice about any individual's screening decisions
practical: Whenever you see a percentage change, ask: change from what baseline, out of how many people?
Bring the absolute numbers, not just the headline, to any conversation with your care team

title: Epidemiology. Environment and disease risks.
headline: A call to measure exposure as systematically as genes are measured -- across a whole life, from inside the body.
summary_short: This perspective argued that a new paradigm is needed to assess how a lifetime of exposure to environmental factors affects the risk of chronic disease -- a framing that helped move the exposome from a concept toward a research programme.
summary_detail:
Genome-wide studies had found that inherited variants explain only part of common chronic diseases. In this short perspective, Rappaport and Smith argued that environmental exposure -- in the broad sense of everything not inherited -- deserves measurement as systematic as the genome's, across a whole lifetime.

They made the case for characterising the exposome from inside the body, by measuring chemicals and their effects in blood, so that exposures from air, water, diet, drugs, infections and the body's own processes are captured together. The paper is widely cited as a turning point in treating the exposome as something to measure rather than only to describe.
key_findings: Calls for a new paradigm to assess lifetime environmental exposure and chronic disease
Argues for measuring exposure inside the body, as systematically as the genome
Helped turn the exposome into a research programme
limitations: A perspective, not a study with new data
Only a one-sentence abstract is indexed on PubMed; this summary reflects the paper's widely cited argument
practical: Genes are part of the story; the exposome is the part that changes

title: Type and timing of menopausal hormone therapy and breast cancer risk: individual participant meta-analysis of the worldwide epidemiological evidence.
first_author: Collaborative Group on Hormonal Factors in Breast Cancer
headline: Five years of menopausal hormone therapy from age 50: about one extra breast cancer per 50 users of estrogen plus daily progestagen, and one per 200 with estrogen alone.
summary_short: Pooling prospective studies of 108,647 postmenopausal women who developed breast cancer, every type of menopausal hormone therapy except vaginal estrogen was linked to excess risk, rising with duration and greater for estrogen-progestagen than estrogen-only preparations.
summary_detail:
Findings on breast cancer and menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) had been inconsistent, with little on long-term effects. The Collaborative Group brought together individual data from all eligible prospective studies, published and unpublished: 108,647 postmenopausal women who developed breast cancer, about half of whom had used MHT.

Every type except vaginal estrogen was associated with excess risk, rising with duration and higher for estrogen plus progestagen than estrogen alone; some excess persisted for more than ten years after stopping, with little after less than a year of use. If largely causal, five years of MHT from age 50 would add, at ages 50 to 69, about one breast cancer for every 50 users of estrogen plus daily progestagen, one per 70 with intermittent progestagen and one per 200 with estrogen alone, for women of average weight in high-income countries. These figures size one side of a decision that also involves MHT's benefits.
key_findings: All MHT types except vaginal estrogen were linked to excess breast cancer risk
5 years from age 50: about 1 extra case per 50 (estrogen + daily progestagen), per 70 (intermittent), per 200 (estrogen alone)
Excess rose with duration and persisted for years after stopping
limitations: Observational studies; the absolute estimates assume the associations are largely causal
The benefits of MHT were outside this analysis
Figures are for women of average weight; they differ with body size
practical: Type, dose and duration are a conversation with a clinician -- never a reason for guilt about past use
Vaginal estrogen was not linked to higher risk

title: Food packaging and bisphenol A and bis(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate exposure: findings from a dietary intervention
headline: After three days of fresh food that wasn't canned or packaged in plastic, five families' urinary BPA fell by about two-thirds and their phthalate breakdown products by about half.
summary_short: Twenty people in five families who usually ate a lot of canned and packaged food switched to three days of fresh food that wasn't canned or plastic-packaged. Their urinary BPA fell about 66% and breakdown products of the phthalate DEHP fell 53-56%.
summary_detail:
Bisphenol A (BPA) and DEHP, a common phthalate, are used in plastics and can linings, and have been linked to endocrine effects in animals and in some human studies. What had not been tested directly was how much of a person's exposure comes from food packaging.

A Silent Spring Institute team recruited 20 people in five families who reported eating a lot of canned and packaged food. They ate their usual diet, then three days of 'fresh foods' that were not canned or packaged in plastic, then returned to their usual diet, with evening urine samples collected across eight days.

During the fresh-food days, urinary BPA fell from a geometric mean of 3.7 to 1.2 ng/mL -- about 66% -- and DEHP metabolites fell 53-56%. The highest values fell furthest: 76% for BPA and 93-96% for DEHP metabolites.

The pattern fits how quickly the body clears these compounds: what you eat and how it is packaged shows up in your own measurements within days. With 20 people and no comparison group, though, the study cannot say how much of the drop came from the packaging itself, or what it means for health.
key_findings: Urinary BPA fell about 66% and DEHP metabolites 53-56% during three fresh-food days
The highest values fell furthest: 76% for BPA, 93-96% for DEHP metabolites
The change showed up within days, not months
limitations: 20 people in 5 families, with no separate comparison group
Three days of change, measured in pooled evening urine samples -- recent exposure, not health outcomes
'Not canned or plastic-packaged' was one bundle of changes, so the study cannot separate packaging from the rest of the diet
practical: A few days of fresh food in place of canned and plastic-packaged food is exactly the change this study tested -- a small experiment you can run yourself
Glass or ceramic containers for storing and heating food sidestep the question of what the plastic contributes

title: Concentrations of parabens in human breast tumours.
headline: Parabens could be measured intact in 20 breast tumour samples -- which showed exposure, not cause, as the authors noted.
summary_short: Using liquid chromatography and tandem mass spectrometry, this study measured parabens in 20 human breast tumours (mean 20.6 ng per gram of tissue, mostly methylparaben). It had no normal tissue to compare, and the authors named that comparison as the next question.
summary_detail:
Parabens are preservatives in many cosmetic, food and pharmaceutical products and show weak estrogen-like activity in laboratory studies. This study asked whether they can persist intact in human tissue at everyday exposure levels. Researchers extracted and measured parabens in samples from 20 human breast tumours, finding a mean of 20.6 ng per gram of tissue, with methylparaben the largest share (62%).

The study showed that parabens can be found intact in breast tissue. It did not compare tumour tissue with normal tissue, and it did not look at product use or cancer occurrence; the authors wrote that the method opens the way to learning whether body burdens differ between cancer and normal tissue. Finding a chemical in tissue is evidence of exposure; whether it plays any part in disease is a separate question this design cannot answer.
key_findings: Parabens measured intact in 20 breast tumour samples, mean 20.6 ng/g
Methylparaben made up about 62% of the total
No normal-tissue comparison, so no conclusion about cause was possible
limitations: Only 20 samples, all from tumours
No comparison with normal tissue or with people's product use
Detection shows exposure, not effect
practical: 'Found in tumours' headlines need the comparison: how much is in normal tissue?
Limiting parabens is easy with labels if you prefer to; harm at everyday levels has not been established

title: An Environment-Wide Association Study (EWAS) on type 2 diabetes mellitus.
headline: Screening 266 environmental factors at once, the way genome studies screen genes, flagged leads for type 2 diabetes -- and showed the limits of the method.
summary_short: Using NHANES data from 1999 to 2006, this pilot environment-wide association study tested 266 factors against type 2 diabetes, controlled for multiple comparisons and checked findings across cohorts, flagging heptachlor epoxide, PCBs and gamma-tocopherol, with beta-carotenes inversely associated.
summary_detail:
Genome-wide association studies scan many genetic variants at once. This pilot applied the same logic to the environment: 266 environmental factors measured in US NHANES participants from 1999 to 2006 were each tested against type 2 diabetes (fasting glucose of 126 mg/dL or more), adjusted for age, sex, body mass index, ethnicity and socioeconomic status, with multiple comparisons controlled and findings checked in other cohorts.

The pesticide breakdown product heptachlor epoxide (odds ratio 1.7 per standard deviation), polychlorinated biphenyls such as PCB170 (2.2) and the vitamin E form gamma-tocopherol (1.5) were associated with diabetes, and beta-carotenes inversely (0.6). The authors stressed how hard it is to establish causality from such data and presented the findings as hypotheses about the environment's broad contribution to disease.
key_findings: 266 environmental factors screened against type 2 diabetes, with multiple-comparison control
Heptachlor epoxide (OR 1.7) and PCB170 (OR 2.2) associated; beta-carotenes inversely (OR 0.6)
Some environmental associations were as large as the strongest genetic findings
limitations: Cross-sectional: exposure and disease were measured at the same time
Single measurements may not reflect long-term exposure
Associations are hypotheses, not shown causes
practical: Screening many exposures at once produces leads to test, not conclusions

title: Screening for Breast Cancer: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement.
headline: USPSTF 2024: a screening mammogram every two years for women aged 40 to 74 at average risk.
summary_short: Based on a systematic review and collaborative modelling, the US Preventive Services Task Force recommends biennial screening mammography for women aged 40 to 74 (grade B), and found the evidence insufficient for women 75 and older and for supplemental ultrasound or MRI in dense breasts (I statements).
summary_detail:
Breast cancer is the second most common cancer and the second most common cause of cancer death among US women; an estimated 43,170 women died of it in 2023, and non-Hispanic Black women have the highest mortality. The Task Force commissioned a systematic review of mammography-based screening strategies -- when to start and stop, how often, which modality, supplemental imaging, personalisation -- together with collaborative modelling studies.

It concluded with moderate certainty that biennial screening mammography from 40 to 74 has a moderate net benefit (grade B). The evidence was insufficient to weigh benefits and harms of screening at 75 and older, or of supplemental ultrasound or MRI for women with dense breasts and an otherwise negative mammogram (I statements). The recommendation applies to people at average risk.
key_findings: Biennial screening mammography for women aged 40 to 74 (grade B)
Insufficient evidence for women 75 and older (I statement)
Insufficient evidence for supplemental ultrasound or MRI in dense breasts (I statement)
limitations: Applies to people at average risk only
Modelling estimates depend on assumptions about tumour growth and treatment
Benefits and harms differ by age and individual history
practical: From 40, talk with a clinician about screening every two years
A family history of breast or ovarian cancer is worth raising -- the plan may differ

title: Risk Assessment, Genetic Counseling, and Genetic Testing for BRCA-Related Cancer: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement.
headline: USPSTF: women whose family history or ancestry suggests a BRCA1/2 variant should be offered a brief assessment, then counseling and, if indicated, testing.
summary_short: Harmful BRCA1/2 variants occur in about 1 in 300 to 500 women and account for 5 to 10% of breast cancers. The Task Force recommends a brief familial risk assessment for women with a relevant personal or family history or ancestry (grade B), and recommends against routine testing for others (grade D).
summary_detail:
Harmful variants in BRCA1 and BRCA2 raise the chance of breast, ovarian, fallopian tube and peritoneal cancer. They occur in an estimated 1 in 300 to 500 women and account for 5% to 10% of breast cancers and 15% of ovarian cancers. The Task Force reviewed evidence on risk assessment, genetic counseling, genetic testing and interventions -- intensive screening, medications and risk-reducing surgery -- for women never diagnosed and for those treated and considered cancer-free.

For women whose personal or family history, or ancestry, is associated with harmful variants, the benefits were judged moderate: primary care clinicians should use a brief familial risk assessment tool, followed by genetic counseling and, if indicated, testing (grade B). For women without such history or ancestry, benefits were small to none, and routine assessment, counseling or testing is not recommended (grade D).
key_findings: BRCA1/2 variants: about 1 in 300 to 500 women; 5-10% of breast and 15% of ovarian cancers
Brief familial risk assessment, then counseling and testing if indicated, for women with relevant history or ancestry (B)
Routine testing is not recommended for women without such history or ancestry (D)
limitations: Focused on BRCA1/2-related cancers
Familial risk assessment tools are brief screens, not diagnoses
A recommendation statement, not a primary study
practical: Gather your family history -- cancers, relatives, ages at diagnosis -- before a clinician visit
Genetic counseling comes before testing, so results can be understood

title: Triclosan exposure, transformation, and human health effects.
journal: J Toxicol Environ Health B Crit Rev
headline: About 75% of Americans carry detectable triclosan in their bodies; the FDA banned it from soap in 2016, but it's still allowed in toothpaste, mouthwash, and surgical antiseptic.
summary_short: A toxicology review found triclosan -- an antimicrobial used in personal care and consumer products since the 1970s -- is readily absorbed through skin and detected in the urine, blood, and breast milk of most Americans tested. After an FDA safety review, triclosan was banned from over-the-counter soap in 2016, but it remains permitted in toothpaste, mouthwash, hand sanitizer, and surgical scrubs. The review summarizes evidence linking triclosan to reproductive and endocrine effects in animal studies, though human evidence is less conclusive.
summary_detail:
Triclosan (TCS) has been used as an antibacterial and antifungal agent in personal care products, textiles, and plastics since the 1970s. Because of how widely it was used, the authors estimate roughly three in four Americans carry a detectable level of triclosan in their body, usually from skin contact with soap, toothpaste, or other treated products.

After reviewing the accumulated evidence, the FDA banned triclosan (and 18 other antibacterial ingredients) from over-the-counter antiseptic soap and body wash in September 2016, on the grounds that manufacturers hadn't shown these ingredients were safe for long-term daily use or more effective than plain soap and water. The ban didn't extend to toothpaste, mouthwash, hand sanitizer, or surgical antiseptic scrubs, where triclosan is still permitted and commonly used.

The review's main focus is the toxicology literature connecting triclosan exposure to reproductive and hormone-system effects, largely from animal studies -- effects on thyroid hormone levels, reproductive development, and estrogen/androgen signaling have been reported at exposure levels above typical human use. The authors are clear that the human evidence for these effects is more limited and mixed than the animal evidence, and call for more research directly in humans.
key_findings: Roughly 75% of Americans tested have detectable triclosan in urine, blood, or breast milk
FDA banned triclosan from OTC soap/body wash in 2016; still permitted in toothpaste, mouthwash, hand sanitizer
Animal studies link triclosan to thyroid, reproductive, and hormone-signaling effects at higher exposure levels
limitations: Most of the hormone/reproductive-effect evidence comes from animal studies, not humans
A narrative review, not a formal meta-analysis -- summarizes the field rather than pooling effect sizes
practical: Checking labels for 'triclosan' is most useful for toothpaste, mouthwash, and hand soap -- the products the 2016 ban didn't cover
This is exactly the kind of low-effort, well-documented swap the Personal care topic in Learn covers

title: Soy food intake and breast cancer survival.
headline: Among 5,042 breast cancer survivors in Shanghai, those eating the most soy had lower recurrence and mortality.
summary_short: In the Shanghai Breast Cancer Survival Study, the highest versus lowest quartile of soy protein intake after diagnosis was associated with lower total mortality (HR 0.71) and recurrence (HR 0.68), in both estrogen-receptor-positive and -negative cancers and with or without tamoxifen.
summary_detail:
Soy foods are rich in isoflavones, plant compounds with weak estrogen-like activity, which raised concern that soy might be harmful after breast cancer or interfere with tamoxifen. This population-based cohort followed 5,042 women in Shanghai diagnosed in 2002 to 2006, assessing diet repeatedly after diagnosis and checking medical records.

Over a median of 3.9 years there were 444 deaths and 534 recurrences or breast cancer deaths. Compared with the lowest quartile of soy protein intake, the highest was associated with lower total mortality (hazard ratio 0.71) and recurrence (0.68): adjusted four-year mortality of 7.4% versus 10.3%, and recurrence of 8.0% versus 11.2%. The pattern held for estrogen-receptor-positive and -negative disease, and in tamoxifen users and non-users.
key_findings: Highest vs lowest soy protein quartile: mortality HR 0.71, recurrence HR 0.68
Four-year mortality 7.4% vs 10.3%; recurrence 8.0% vs 11.2%
Similar in ER-positive and ER-negative cancers, with or without tamoxifen
limitations: Observational: women eating more soy may differ in other ways
Soy eaten as a traditional food in China; supplements were not studied
Median follow-up under four years
practical: Based on this cohort, soy foods need not be avoided after breast cancer
Questions about diet during treatment belong with the care team

title: DDT and breast cancer in young women: new data on the significance of age at exposure.
headline: High DDT levels predicted about five times the odds of breast cancer before 50 -- but only in women first exposed as children.
summary_short: Using blood drawn from young mothers in Oakland, California, in 1959-1967, high p,p'-DDT predicted a five-fold increase in breast cancer before age 50 among women born after 1931 -- under 14 when DDT came into wide use -- and no association among women exposed only later.
summary_detail:
Earlier studies of DDT and breast cancer measured exposure late in life, after most DDT had been eliminated and long after its use had stopped, and mostly found no link. This study used blood samples saved by the Child Health and Development Studies, drawn one to three days after women gave birth in 1959-1967 (mean age 26), during the years of peak DDT use.

Comparing 129 women who developed breast cancer before 50 with 129 controls matched by birth year, high serum p,p'-DDT predicted a statistically significant five-fold increase in risk among women born after 1931, who were under 14 when DDT came into widespread use in 1945. Women not exposed before 14 showed no association. The study points to childhood and adolescence as a window of susceptibility, and shows how measuring exposure at the wrong time can hide an effect.
key_findings: Five-fold higher odds of breast cancer before 50 with high p,p'-DDT -- for women exposed before age 14
No association for women first exposed later in life
The timing of exposure changed the result entirely
limitations: 129 cases: a small study with wide uncertainty
A single blood measurement around childbirth
DDT is no longer in general use in the US, so today's exposures are far lower
practical: Exposures in childhood and adolescence deserve extra care
A 'no link' study that measured exposure late in life may have missed the window that mattered

title: Proportion and number of cancer cases and deaths attributable to potentially modifiable risk factors in the United States, 2019.
headline: 40% of cancer cases and 44% of cancer deaths in US adults 30 and over were attributable to potentially modifiable factors in 2019.
summary_short: Combining national cancer data, risk-factor prevalence and published relative risks, the American Cancer Society estimated that 713,340 cancer cases (40.0%) and 262,120 deaths (44.0%) in 2019 were attributable to factors led by smoking (19.3% of cases), excess body weight (7.6%) and alcohol (5.4%).
summary_detail:
Updating an estimate for 2014, the authors calculated how many invasive cancers (excluding non-melanoma skin cancer) and cancer deaths among US adults aged 30 and over in 2019 were attributable to cigarette smoking, second-hand smoke, excess body weight, alcohol, red and processed meat, low intake of fruits, vegetables, fiber and calcium, physical inactivity, ultraviolet radiation and seven carcinogenic infections.

In total, 40.0% of cases (713,340 of 1,781,649) and 44.0% of deaths (262,120 of 595,737) were attributable to these factors. Cigarette smoking contributed most (19.3% of cases, 28.5% of deaths), followed by excess body weight (7.6%, 7.3%) and alcohol (5.4%, 4.1%). For 19 of 30 cancer types more than half of cases were attributable, and female breast cancer had 83,840 attributable cases. These are population estimates of where prevention can help, not explanations of any individual's cancer.
key_findings: 40.0% of cases and 44.0% of deaths attributable to the factors evaluated
Smoking 19.3% of cases; excess body weight 7.6%; alcohol 5.4%
83,840 attributable female breast cancer cases
limitations: Depends on relative risks from other studies and on survey-based prevalence
Factors outside the list, including many occupational and environmental exposures, were not evaluated
A population fraction: it cannot say why a given person developed cancer
practical: The biggest levers are few: smoke-free air, alcohol, body weight, activity, vaccines, sun
Population estimates are for planning prevention, never for assigning blame

title: Evaluation of Maternal, Embryo, and Placental Effects in CD-1 Mice following Gestational Exposure to Perfluorooctanoic Acid (PFOA) or Hexafluoropropylene Oxide Dimer Acid (HFPO-DA or GenX).
headline: GenX, the short-chain PFAS marketed as a faster-clearing PFOA replacement, produced many of the same effects as PFOA in pregnant mice head-to-head -- despite its much shorter half-life.
summary_short: NIEHS and EPA researchers dosed pregnant mice with either PFOA (the older, restricted 'long-chain' PFAS) or GenX (its short-chain replacement, promoted as safer partly because it clears the body faster) and compared effects on the mother, placenta, and embryo. GenX reproduced many of PFOA's documented effects, including maternal liver changes and placental abnormalities, despite its shorter half-life.
summary_detail:
As PFOA and other long-chain PFAS drew regulatory restriction for their extreme persistence (serum half-lives measured in years) and health associations, manufacturers moved to short-chain alternatives like GenX (HFPO-DA), promoted partly on the grounds that a shorter half-life should mean less cumulative exposure and therefore less risk.

This study tested that assumption directly: pregnant CD-1 mice were dosed with either PFOA or GenX at comparable levels from early to mid-late gestation, then maternal liver histopathology, placental histopathology, embryo/placental weight, and placental thyroid hormone levels were measured and compared.

Both chemicals produced elevated gestational weight gain, higher maternal liver weights, changes in liver histopathology, and a greater incidence of placental abnormalities relative to unexposed controls, with effect sizes similar between the two chemicals at comparable doses.
