Some placental effects showed compound-specific patterns, suggesting the two aren't biologically identical -- but the overall conclusion was that GenX 'recapitulated many documented effects of PFOA... regardless of its much shorter reported half-life.' A faster-clearing replacement didn't translate into a cleanly better safety profile in this head-to-head comparison.
key_findings: GenX and PFOA produced similar increases in gestational weight gain and maternal liver weight at comparable doses
Both chemicals increased the incidence of placental abnormalities relative to controls
GenX's much shorter half-life did not prevent it from reproducing many of PFOA's documented effects
limitations: A mouse study -- species differences in PFAS handling are well documented, so human potency may differ
Tests one exposure window and route (oral gavage during gestation); doesn't cover other life stages or routes
practical: PFAS exposure reduction habits (retiring worn non-stick pans, not eating directly from grease-resistant wrappers) are about the whole chemical class, not just the specific compounds a package might name
"Shorter half-life" and "safer" aren't the same claim -- this is the concrete study behind that distinction

title: Toxicological interactions of pesticide mixtures: an update.
headline: Most real-world chemical mixtures add up roughly as expected from their individual doses -- true synergy (the combination doing more damage than the sum of its parts) shows up mainly at unrealistically high lab concentrations, not everyday exposure levels.
summary_short: A review of how pesticides interact when combined found that while synergistic interactions (where a mixture is more toxic than its components' doses added together) are real and documented -- especially among cholinesterase-inhibiting insecticides and certain fungicides -- the available evidence suggests they're rare at the concentrations people actually encounter through diet or environment, and mostly appear in lab studies using much higher doses.
summary_detail:
When two or more chemicals are present together, their combined effect can be additive (roughly the sum of each one's effect), synergistic (more than the sum -- one chemical amplifies the other), or antagonistic (less than the sum -- one blunts the other). Regulatory cumulative risk assessment generally assumes additivity within a 'common mechanism group' (chemicals that act through the same biological pathway) as a protective default.

This review surveyed the pesticide-mixture literature specifically. It found synergistic interactions are real and mechanistically explainable -- most often because one chemical interferes with how the body metabolizes/clears another, amplifying its effective dose. Cholinesterase-inhibiting insecticides, triazole fungicides, triazine herbicides, and pyrethroids showed up disproportionately in documented synergistic pairs.

The important caveat for everyday exposure: the authors note that synergisms have mostly been demonstrated at experimentally high concentrations, and the limited evidence available suggests synergism at typical dietary exposure levels is rare. That doesn't mean mixtures don't matter -- it means the additive-default assumption regulators use is a reasonably protective starting point, not a claim that combined exposure is risk-free.
key_findings: Combined chemical effects can be additive, synergistic (more than additive), or antagonistic (less than additive), depending on the specific pair and mechanism
Synergistic interactions are usually explained by one chemical altering how the body metabolizes the other, effectively raising its dose
Documented synergisms mostly occurred at high experimental concentrations; evidence suggests synergism at typical real-world dietary exposure levels is rare
limitations: Focused specifically on pesticide-pesticide interactions, not the full range of everyday chemical mixtures (food additives, personal-care ingredients, etc.)
A narrative review of the existing literature, not a new quantitative risk assessment
practical: Reducing the number of different flagged sources in a routine (not just the amount of any one) is the practical takeaway behind cumulative/aggregate exposure thinking in this app
Regulatory limits for a chemical class (like organophosphates) are generally set assuming additive combined exposure across the group, which is the protective, conservative assumption

title: Reducing phthalate, paraben, and phenol exposure from personal care products in adolescent girls: findings from the HERMOSA intervention study
headline: Three days of personal care products labelled free of phthalates, parabens, triclosan and BP-3 lowered most of those chemicals in 100 teenagers' urine by a quarter to a half -- and two other parabens unexpectedly rose.
summary_short: One hundred Latina teenagers used personal care products labelled free of phthalates, parabens, triclosan and benzophenone-3 for three days. Monoethyl phthalate fell about 27%, methyl and propyl paraben about 44-45%, triclosan about 36% and benzophenone-3 about 36% -- while ethyl and butyl paraben unexpectedly rose.
summary_detail:
Personal care products -- cosmetics, lotions, shampoos, sunscreens -- can be a source of chemicals such as phthalates, parabens, triclosan and benzophenone-3 (BP-3), which are suspected endocrine disruptors. The HERMOSA study asked whether ordinary consumer choices could change that.

It was designed with teenagers, not only for them: 100 Latina girls took part in a youth-led, community-based intervention. For three days they used products whose labels said they did not contain the target chemicals, and urine collected before and after was analysed for the chemicals and their metabolites.

On average, monoethyl phthalate (MEP) fell 27.4%, methyl paraben 43.9% and propyl paraben 45.4%, triclosan 35.7% and BP-3 36.0%. Two other phthalate metabolites did not change significantly, and ethyl and butyl paraben concentrations actually rose -- at low overall levels, and undetected in almost half the samples.

The authors' conclusion is measured: label-based choices available to any shopper can lower personal exposure to these chemicals. They also credit involving young people in the design with the study's recruitment, retention and compliance.
key_findings: MEP fell 27.4%; methyl and propyl paraben fell about 44-45%; triclosan and BP-3 fell about 36%
Two phthalate metabolites (MnBP, MiBP) did not change significantly
Ethyl and butyl paraben rose -- unexpected, and at low levels
limitations: Before-and-after design over three days, with no comparison group
Urine levels reflect recent exposure, not long-term burden or health outcomes
Products were chosen by their label claims, and the rise in two parabens shows a swap does not lower everything
practical: Read the ingredient list, not just the front of the pack: 'fragrance-free' and 'unscented' are not the same thing
When you swap away from one chemical, watch for its relatives -- the same reason this app groups related compounds together

title: Radiation-Induced Breast Cancer Incidence and Mortality From Digital Mammography Screening: A Modeling Study.
headline: Yearly mammograms from 40 to 74: about 125 radiation-induced breast cancers per 100,000 women, against about 968 breast cancer deaths averted.
summary_short: Two simulation models estimated that annual digital mammography for 100,000 women aged 40 to 74 would induce about 125 breast cancers and 16 deaths through radiation, while averting 968 breast cancer deaths; biennial screening from 50 cut radiation-induced cancers five-fold.
summary_detail:
Earlier estimates of radiation-induced breast cancer from mammography had not accounted for variation in dose between women or for the extra imaging that follows abnormal results. Using two simulation models of the US population, the authors estimated lifetime benefits and radiation harms of annual or biennial digital screening starting at 40, 45 or 50 and continuing to 74.

Annual screening of 100,000 women from 40 to 74 was projected to induce 125 breast cancers leading to 16 deaths, against 968 breast cancer deaths averted by early detection. Women receiving higher doses -- including the 8% with large breasts who need extra views -- had greater projected harm (266 cases and 35 deaths per 100,000). Biennial screening starting at 50 reduced radiation-induced cancers five-fold. Dose, frequency and starting age all shape the balance.
key_findings: Annual screening 40-74: 125 radiation-induced cancers and 16 deaths vs 968 deaths averted, per 100,000
Higher-dose groups, such as women needing extra views, had greater projected harm
Biennial screening from 50 cut radiation-induced cancers five-fold
limitations: Model-based estimates, not observed cancers
Life-years lost from radiation-induced cancer could not be estimated
Results depend on dose assumptions that vary between women
practical: A mammogram's radiation dose is small and the benefit larger -- dose-response, applied
How often and from what age to screen are part of the decision to discuss with a clinician

title: Effect of organic diet intervention on pesticide exposures in young children living in low-income urban and agricultural communities
headline: Seven days of organic food lowered urinary markers of organophosphate insecticides by 40-49%, and of the herbicide 2,4-D by 25%, in 40 young children.
summary_short: Forty Mexican-American children aged 3-6 in California ate conventionally grown food for 4 days, organic food for 7, then conventional again for 5. During the organic days, markers of organophosphate insecticides fell 40-49% and of the herbicide 2,4-D 25%; several other pesticide markers were rarely detected or unchanged.
summary_detail:
Earlier organic-diet studies had mostly involved children in suburban communities. This one followed 40 Mexican-American children aged 3-6 living in low-income urban (Oakland) and agricultural (Salinas) communities in California, where home and farm-related exposures can differ.

Over 16 consecutive days the children ate conventionally grown food for 4 days, organic food for 7 days, then conventionally grown food for 5 days, while urine samples were analysed for 23 pesticide metabolites -- organophosphate, pyrethroid and others.

Of the six metabolites detected often enough to analyse, levels during the organic phase were generally lower. The reductions were statistically significant for total dialkylphosphates (-40%) and dimethyl dialkylphosphates (-49%), both markers of organophosphate insecticides, and for 2,4-D (-25%). Several chemical-specific pyrethroid and herbicide metabolites were rarely detected or not significantly changed. Levels for most frequently detected metabolites were generally higher in Salinas than in Oakland.

The authors note that diet is one source among several, and that more research is needed to sort out how much comes from food versus the home and other routes.
key_findings: Organophosphate insecticide markers fell 40% (total DAPs) and 49% (dimethyl DAPs) on the organic diet
The herbicide 2,4-D marker fell 25%
Several pyrethroid and herbicide markers were rarely detected or unchanged
limitations: 40 children over 16 days; each child was their own comparison, with no separate control group
Urine markers show recent exposure, not health effects
Diet was one source of several -- the study cannot say how much came from the home or elsewhere
practical: If organic isn't within reach, the produce guide in this app (higher-residue 'watch list' versus lower-residue items) is a practical way to choose where to put the effort
Diet is one route; home and garden products are another, so the two add up

title: The IARC Monographs: Updated Procedures for Modern and Transparent Evidence Synthesis in Cancer Hazard Identification.
headline: How IARC decides whether something can cause cancer: three streams of evidence, integrated in one step -- and what the result does and does not mean.
summary_short: This paper describes IARC's 2019 updated Preamble: stronger systematic review methods, more weight on mechanistic evidence organised by the key characteristics of carcinogens, closer scrutiny of exposure assessment in human studies, and single-step integration of human, animal and mechanistic evidence.
summary_detail:
The International Agency for Research on Cancer's Monographs identify agents that can cause cancer in humans -- hazard identification, the first step in cancer prevention. In 2019 the Preamble that governs the process was updated on the recommendation of an expert advisory group, the first major amendment in 12 years.

The update strengthens systematic review methods; gives more weight to mechanistic evidence organised around the key characteristics of carcinogens; looks harder at the quality and informativeness of epidemiological studies, including how exposure was assessed; harmonises evaluation criteria across evidence streams; and integrates evidence on cancer in humans, cancer in experimental animals and mechanisms in a single step to reach an overall classification. IARC states separately that the resulting groups indicate the strength of the evidence, not the level of risk at a given exposure.
key_findings: IARC classifies the strength of evidence that an agent can cause cancer (hazard)
Three evidence streams -- human, animal, mechanistic -- integrated in one step
The 2019 update strengthened systematic review and the use of mechanistic evidence
limitations: Hazard identification only: it does not estimate risk at a given dose
A procedures paper; the classifications themselves are in the Monographs
Authors include IARC staff and working-group members
practical: When a headline says 'carcinogen', ask which group and what exposure the evidence involved
Agents in the same group can differ greatly in how much cancer they cause

title: Exposure data for cosmetic products: facial cleanser, hair conditioner, and eye shadow.
headline: How much product do people actually use? In a US diary study, women used about 14 g of hair conditioner a day -- and 0.04 g of eye shadow.
summary_short: 360 US women aged 18 to 69 weighed and logged their usual facial cleanser, hair conditioner and eye shadow for two weeks. Mean daily use was about 4.1 g, 13.8 g and 0.04 g, at 1.1 to 1.6 applications a day -- the kind of data safety assessments use to estimate dose.
summary_detail:
Safety assessments of cosmetic ingredients need two numbers: how much product is applied and how often. To update them, 360 women aged 18 to 69 across the US who regularly used facial cleanser, hair conditioner or eye shadow were given a new container of their usual brand, kept diaries for two weeks, and had their products weighed before and after.

Mean use per application was 2.57 g for facial cleanser, 13.13 g for hair conditioner and 0.03 g for eye shadow; per day it was 4.06 g, 13.77 g and 0.04 g, with 1.6, 1.1 and 1.2 applications a day. The several-hundredfold spread between products is why exposure assessments start from real use patterns rather than from whether an ingredient is present.
key_findings: Mean daily use: facial cleanser 4.06 g, hair conditioner 13.77 g, eye shadow 0.04 g
1.1 to 1.6 applications a day
Daily amounts differed several hundredfold between products
limitations: Three product types only
Industry-affiliated authors (a cosmetics trade association)
Regular users of these products, not a random population sample
practical: Products used in large amounts, and those left on the skin, are where swaps move the most
Amount and frequency matter as much as the ingredient list

title: Antiperspirant use and the risk of breast cancer.
headline: A rumour tested: among 1,606 women, antiperspirant and deodorant use were not linked to breast cancer -- shaving included.
summary_short: This population-based case-control study compared 813 women with breast cancer and 793 controls aged 20 to 74. Breast cancer risk did not increase with antiperspirant (OR 0.9) or deodorant (OR 1.2) use, with blade shaving, or with application within an hour of shaving.
summary_detail:
The claim that antiperspirants cause breast cancer circulated widely online, but no epidemiological study had tested it. Researchers in the Seattle area interviewed 813 women diagnosed with breast cancer in 1992-1995 and 793 population controls of similar age, asking in person about their use of underarm products and their shaving habits.

Breast cancer risk did not rise with antiperspirant use (odds ratio 0.9) or deodorant use (1.2, not statistically significant), among women who shaved with a blade razor, or with applying products within an hour of shaving. The authors concluded that the findings do not support the hypothesis that antiperspirant use increases breast cancer risk.
key_findings: Antiperspirant use: odds ratio 0.9 -- no increase
Deodorant use: odds ratio 1.2, not statistically significant
No increase with blade shaving or application soon after shaving
limitations: Self-reported product use, recalled in interviews
Case-control design in one US region in the 1990s
practical: This study does not support the worry; skin irritation after shaving is the better-established issue

title: The U.S. National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey and human exposure to environmental chemicals.
headline: How the US measures what is in people: NHANES biomonitoring sets reference ranges and tracks trends in environmental chemicals.
summary_short: This overview from CDC describes how NHANES, which examines a representative sample of the US population and collects blood and urine, is used to measure environmental chemicals -- setting reference ranges, providing exposure data for risk assessment and monitoring exposure trends.
summary_detail:
Human biomonitoring measures chemicals, their metabolites or reaction products in blood, urine and other specimens. NHANES, run by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, combines a physical examination, a detailed medical history and the collection of biological specimens from people representing the non-institutionalised civilian US population.

Those specimens allow CDC to measure environmental chemicals across the population: to set reference ranges that show what typical levels look like, to supply exposure data for risk assessment, and to follow trends over time -- for example, whether levels fall after a chemical is phased out. Biomonitoring shows exposure; on its own, it does not show harm.
key_findings: NHANES collects blood and urine from a representative US sample
Biomonitoring data set reference ranges for environmental chemicals
Repeated surveys track exposure trends over time
limitations: A programme description rather than a study with results
Biomonitoring shows exposure, not effect
For short-lived chemicals, a single sample reflects only recent exposure
practical: 'Detected in Americans' is a statement about exposure; meaning depends on amounts and comparisons

title: Controversy around parabens: Alternative strategies for preservative use in cosmetics and personal care products.
headline: The common paraben alternatives -- phenoxyethanol, formaldehyde-releasers, triclosan, isothiazolinones -- each carry their own documented adverse-effect profile; none is simply a safety upgrade.
summary_short: A review of preservative strategies in cosmetics surveyed the chemicals most often used in place of parabens -- phenoxyethanol, formaldehyde-releasing preservatives, triclosan, methylisothiazolinone, benzyl alcohol, and sodium benzoate -- and found each has documented adverse effects of its own, from skin sensitization to the specific endocrine and antimicrobial-resistance concerns already tracked for triclosan in this app.
summary_detail:
Parabens' safety has been debated for years, driving many 'paraben-free' reformulations. This review takes stock of what those reformulations typically use instead: phenoxyethanol, formaldehyde-releasing preservatives, triclosan, methylisothiazolinone/methylchloroisothiazolinone, benzyl alcohol, and sodium benzoate are named as the most common substitutes.

The authors' point is not that parabens are vindicated, but that none of the common alternatives is a clean upgrade: each has its own adverse-effect profile in the literature (contact sensitization and allergy for the isothiazolinones in particular, formaldehyde release as a known carcinogen concern, triclosan's endocrine and antimicrobial-resistance questions already covered elsewhere in this library). Interest in plant-based/essential-oil antimicrobials is growing but faces its own effectiveness and formulation challenges at present.

Phenoxyethanol specifically is one of the more commonly used and, per this and other reviews, comparatively lower-concern options at typical cosmetic-use levels -- but 'comparatively lower-concern' is a different claim from 'inert,' and it's a genuinely different chemical with its own limits, not a neutral placeholder for 'paraben-free.'
key_findings: Phenoxyethanol, formaldehyde-releasers, triclosan, and isothiazolinones are the most common paraben substitutes in current cosmetics
Each alternative preservative has its own documented adverse-effect profile in the literature, not a clean safety improvement over parabens
Isothiazolinones (e.g. methylisothiazolinone) are specifically flagged for contact-sensitization/allergy risk
limitations: A narrative review summarizing the field, not a new head-to-head safety comparison with pooled effect sizes
Natural/plant-based alternatives are noted as promising but under-studied for real-world formulation use
practical: 'Paraben-free' describes what's absent, not what replaced it -- worth a glance at the actual ingredient list if minimizing preservative exposure broadly (not just parabens) is the goal
Rotating personal care brands, rather than relying on one 'paraben-free' product exclusively, still applies here

title: Hair dye and chemical straightener use and breast cancer risk in a large US population of black and white women.
headline: In the Sister Study, permanent hair dye was linked to higher breast cancer risk, especially among Black women, and straighteners with more frequent use.
summary_short: Following 46,709 women aged 35 to 74 who had a sister with breast cancer, permanent dye use was associated with 45% higher breast cancer risk in Black women (HR 1.45) and 7% in white women (HR 1.07), and personal straightener use with higher risk (HR 1.18) that rose with frequency.
summary_detail:
Many hair products contain compounds that may be relevant to breast cancer, and products used mainly by Black women may contain more hormonally active ingredients. The Sister Study enrolled 46,709 women aged 35 to 74 in 2003-2009, each free of breast cancer but with a sister who had been diagnosed, and asked about hair product use in the previous year.

Over a mean of 8.3 years, 2,794 breast cancers were diagnosed. Permanent dye use was associated with 45% higher risk among Black women (hazard ratio 1.45) and 7% among white women (1.07, borderline). Personal straightener use was associated with higher risk (1.18) that increased with frequency, and applying semipermanent dye (1.28) or straighteners (1.27) to others outside a salon was also associated. These are observational associations that call for further study.
key_findings: Permanent dye: HR 1.45 among Black women, 1.07 among white women
Personal straightener use: HR 1.18, rising with frequency
Non-professional application to others was also associated
limitations: All participants had a sister with breast cancer, so results may not generalise
Product use asked about only for the 12 months before enrolment
Observational; specific chemicals were not measured
practical: A real signal worth weighing, not settled proof
If you use these products often, frequency is one lever within reach

title: Trends and current spectrum of contact allergy in Central Europe: results of the Information Network of Departments of Dermatology (IVDK) 2007-2018.
headline: Among 125,436 patch-tested patients, fragrance was the second most common contact allergen -- and an allergy wave fell after European regulation.
summary_short: Analysing patch tests at 56 dermatology departments in three Central European countries (2007-2018), the most common allergens were nickel (14.7%), fragrance mix I (8.1%), Myroxylon pereirae resin (7.5%) and cobalt (5.2%); allergy to methylisothiazolinone rose and fell following European regulation.
summary_detail:
Surveillance of patch-test results shows how changing exposures change allergy patterns. The Information Network of Departments of Dermatology pooled results for 125,436 patients tested with the baseline series at 56 departments in three Central European countries between 2007 and 2018.

The most common allergens were nickel (14.7%), fragrance mix I (8.1%), Myroxylon pereirae resin (balsam of Peru, 7.5%) and cobalt (5.2%), with no conclusive trend. Allergy to the preservative methylchloroisothiazolinone/methylisothiazolinone rose and then fell, reflecting an epidemic and its decline after regulation and self-regulation in the European Union. The authors note that decreases in sensitization likely reflect reduced exposure, with some lag.
key_findings: Nickel 14.7%, fragrance mix I 8.1%, balsam of Peru 7.5% among patch-tested patients
The methylisothiazolinone allergy epidemic rose and fell after EU action
Falling sensitization tends to follow reduced exposure, with a lag
limitations: Patients referred for patch testing, not the general population
Central Europe only
Descriptive surveillance
practical: Fragrance allergy is common; patch testing can identify the specific ingredient
Reducing exposure works, even for allergy

title: Ultra-processed food consumption and human health: an umbrella review of systematic reviews with meta-analyses.
headline: Each extra 50 g/day of ultra-processed food tracked with about 2% higher all-cause mortality risk across 16 pooled reviews -- modest, and it's still unclear if processing itself is the cause.
summary_short: An umbrella review pooled 16 systematic reviews and meta-analyses on ultra-processed (NOVA-defined) food and health outcomes. Moderate-certainty evidence linked higher intake to higher all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, and colorectal cancer, rising gradually with intake. The authors note it's still unclear whether processing itself drives the risk, or whether ultra-processed intake is mostly a marker of a lower-quality diet overall.
summary_detail:
Researchers searched four databases through January 2024 for systematic reviews with meta-analyses that used the NOVA classification system to define ultra-processed food, then combined their results and rated the certainty of each finding using GRADE -- the same framework used to grade clinical guidelines.

Sixteen publications were included. Moderate-certainty evidence linked higher ultra-processed food intake to higher all-cause mortality (about 2% higher risk per extra 50 g/day), cardiovascular disease incidence and mortality (4-5% higher per 50 g/day), type 2 diabetes incidence (12% higher per 10 percentage points of diet), and colorectal cancer (4% higher per 10 percentage points). Similar patterns showed up for obesity, metabolic syndrome, fatty liver disease, and mental health outcomes, but the evidence behind those was weaker.

The authors are candid about a key limitation: because NOVA classifies food by how it's processed rather than by nutrient content, it's hard to separate the effect of processing itself from the fact that most ultra-processed diets are also higher in sugar, refined starch, and sodium, and lower in fiber. This is one of the largest, most rigorously graded syntheses on the topic to date -- but it's built from observational associations, not proof that processing itself is the cause.
key_findings: 2% higher all-cause mortality risk per extra 50 g/day of ultra-processed food (moderate certainty)
4-5% higher cardiovascular disease incidence/mortality per 50 g/day (moderate certainty)
12% higher type 2 diabetes incidence per 10 percentage points of diet (moderate certainty)
limitations: Built from observational cohorts, not randomized trials -- shows association, not proof of cause
Can't fully separate 'food processing' from 'a diet that's also higher in sugar, refined starch, and sodium'
practical: The starter quests' cereal-aisle swap and label-reading habit both target this exact pattern
Pairs with the Hall et al. 2019 trial in this library, which shows a mechanism: people eat more calories, unprompted, on ultra-processed menus

title: The significance of batch and patch test method in establishing contact allergy to fragrance mix I-EDEN Fragrance Study Group.
headline: In a random sample of 3,119 European adults, between 0.7% and 2.6% were allergic to a standard fragrance mix -- depending on the test used.
summary_short: The EDEN Fragrance Study patch-tested 3,119 people from the general population in five European countries with two batches of fragrance mix I and two test techniques. Allergy prevalence ranged from 0.7% to 2.6%, varying with the oak moss content of the mix and the testing method.
summary_detail:
Fragrance mix I, a blend of eight fragrance ingredients, is part of most baseline patch-test series. To see how much the batch of the mix and the test technique matter, the EDEN Fragrance Study patch-tested 3,119 people from the general population at six dermatology clinics in five European countries, using two batches and two techniques.

The prevalence of contact allergy to the mix ranged from 0.7% to 2.6%. Mixes whose oak moss (Evernia prunastri) contained more chloroatranol and atranol produced substantially more positive reactions, and the Finn Chamber technique detected more allergy than the TRUE Test. A prevalence figure is only as good as the test behind it -- and in the general population, fragrance allergy is real but far less common than among patients referred to dermatologists.
key_findings: Fragrance mix I allergy in the general population: 0.7% to 2.6%
Oak moss content changed how many people reacted
The Finn Chamber method detected more allergy than the TRUE Test
limitations: Test method and batch strongly affect the estimate
Five European countries only
Fragrance mix I covers eight ingredients, not all fragrance chemicals
practical: How common an allergy looks depends on who is tested and how
A dermatologist's patch test is the way to find a personal fragrance allergy

title: Bra wearing not associated with breast cancer risk: a population-based case-control study.
headline: No aspect of bra wearing -- cup size, hours a day, underwires, age at first wearing -- was linked to breast cancer in women aged 55 to 74.
summary_short: Comparing 454 women with invasive ductal carcinoma and 590 with invasive lobular carcinoma against 469 controls aged 55 to 74 in the Seattle area, no aspect of bra wearing, including underwires, hours per day or age at first regular use, was associated with either cancer type.
summary_detail:
Lay media had suggested that wearing a bra might raise breast cancer risk, but credible studies were scarce. This population-based case-control study in the Seattle-Puget Sound area compared 454 women with invasive ductal carcinoma and 590 with invasive lobular carcinoma, diagnosed in 2000-2004, with 469 control women aged 55 to 74, collecting bra-wearing habits and other factors in in-person interviews.

No aspect of bra wearing -- cup size, how recently or how many hours a day bras were worn, underwires, or the age at which women began wearing them regularly -- was associated with the risk of either cancer type. The results did not support the claim that bra wearing increases breast cancer risk.
key_findings: No association with cup size, hours worn per day or underwires
No association with age at first regular bra wearing
Held for both ductal and lobular breast cancers
limitations: Postmenopausal women aged 55 to 74 only
Self-reported habits
One US metropolitan area
practical: Based on this evidence, bra choice is about comfort, not breast cancer

title: Levers to decrease exposure to harmful chemicals: the case of personal care products and cosmetics
study_type: Intervention study with health impact assessment
headline: Five days of swapping personal care products lowered urinary markers of phenoxyethanol (about 64%), BPA, methylparaben and a phthalate in 103 young women -- and the authors add that regulation would do more than individual choices.
summary_short: In Grenoble, 103 women aged 18-30 set aside their usual personal care products for five days and used alternatives free of the chemicals of interest. Urinary phenoxyacetic acid (a breakdown product of phenoxyethanol) fell about 64%, BPA 39%, methylparaben 30% and monoethyl phthalate 22%.
summary_detail:
Personal care products can be a modifiable source of chemical exposure -- but how much can a person change by changing what they use? This 2026 study tested it directly. In Grenoble, France, 103 women aged 18-30 gave up their usual products for five days and were given alternatives free of the chemicals being measured (eleven phenols, sixteen phthalates and two glycol ethers). They used a median of 12 products a day beforehand and 7 during the intervention.

Comparing 24-hour urine collections from before and from the last intervention day, median phenoxyacetic acid -- a breakdown product of the preservative phenoxyethanol -- fell 64%, bisphenol A 39%, methylparaben 30% and monoethyl phthalate 22%, and propylparaben was detected less often. Several chemicals were still detectable afterwards: personal care products are one source among several.

The team also ran a health impact assessment, a modelling exercise, for bisphenol A in pregnancy. Its estimates were uncertain, and they are best read as a hypothesis rather than a finding. The authors' own conclusion is worth keeping in view: individual changes can lower exposure, but regulatory action would probably be more efficient and fairer.
key_findings: Phenoxyacetic acid fell 64%, BPA 39%, methylparaben 30% and monoethyl phthalate 22% after five days
Products used per day fell from a median of 12 to 7
Several chemicals were still detectable after the swap
limitations: Very recent (2026): not yet widely cited or independently replicated
Five days, before-and-after, women aged 18-30 in one city, with no comparison group
The health impact estimates are modelled rather than observed, and uncertain
practical: Fewer products and simpler ingredient lists both mattered here: participants went from 12 products a day to 7
Personal choices help, and shared measures such as labelling and regulation reach further -- both can be true at once

title: Review of the standards of proof (of safety) for FDA regulated consumer products and how the generally recognized as safe criteria could be applied to cosmetics.
headline: MoCRA raised the safety standard for US cosmetics to a 'reasonable certainty' of safety -- the same bar as food ingredients.
summary_short: This review explains that the Modernization of Cosmetics Regulation Act of 2022 raises the standard of proof of safety for cosmetics to a 'reasonable certainty' that a product is safe, equal to that for food ingredients, and compares the standards across FDA-regulated product types.
summary_detail:
Different FDA-regulated products must meet different 'standards of proof' of safety. The Modernization of Cosmetics Regulation Act of 2022 amended the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act and raised the standard for cosmetics to a 'reasonable certainty' of safety -- the same standard that applies to food ingredients.

The author describes the standards for cosmetics, dietary supplements, food ingredients and foods, compares them with familiar legal terms such as 'a preponderance of the evidence' and 'beyond reasonable doubt', ranks them by how hard they are to meet, and suggests how the generally-recognised-as-safe approach used for food ingredients could help companies meet the higher bar for cosmetics.
key_findings: MoCRA set a 'reasonable certainty' safety standard for cosmetics
That standard matches the one for food ingredients
Standards of proof differ across FDA-regulated product types
limitations: A single-author regulatory analysis, not a study with data
The author works for a regulatory consultancy
How FDA will apply the standard in practice is still developing
practical: Companies must now keep evidence that their products are safe
FDA still does not approve most cosmetics before sale; color additives are the exception
